title: 2 Chronicles 11:1–17
context: Rehoboam gathers 180,000 men of Judah and Benjamin to reunite the kingdom by force, but the LORD’s word through Shemaiah forbids war against their brothers, “for this thing is of me,” and they obey (11:1–4; parallel 1 Kings 12:21–24). The rest of the unit has no parallel in Kings. Rehoboam fortifies cities throughout Judah and Benjamin (11:5–12). Priests and Levites from all Israel, cast off by Jeroboam, leave their lands and come to Judah and Jerusalem, followed by people from every tribe who set their hearts to seek the LORD (11:13–16). Chronicles adds goat idols to the calf idols that 1 Kings 12:28 describes. For three years these newcomers strengthen the kingdom, while Judah walks in the way of David and Solomon (11:17). Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: obedience to God’s word prevents bloodshed, and faithful worshipers who seek the LORD strengthen his people.

verses.text: When Rehoboam had come to Jerusalem, he assembled the house of Judah and Benjamin, one hundred eighty thousand chosen men who were warriors, to fight against Israel, to bring the kingdom again to Rehoboam.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam gathers 180,000 chosen warriors from Judah and Benjamin to restore the kingdom by force. Arminian readers see a king responding to loss with a plan for war. His decision is understandable but stands against God’s purpose, as the next verses reveal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a king about to act against what God has ordained. The number matches 1 Kings 12:21. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse plainly, noting Benjamin’s place with Judah and Rehoboam’s determination to reverse the division.

verses.text: But the LORD’s word came to Shemaiah the man of God, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to Shemaiah the man of God. Arminian readers note that God speaks at the critical moment, giving Rehoboam the opportunity to turn back before bloodshed. A prophet’s word confronts the king’s plan.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God intervening through his prophet to restrain the king. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of God’s gracious guidance through the prophetic word, which the king and people will be responsible to heed.

verses.text: “Speak to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Israel in Judah and Benjamin, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Shemaiah is to speak to Rehoboam and to all Israel in Judah and Benjamin. Arminian readers note that the message addresses the people as well as the king. Everyone involved in the planned war is called to hear and obey the LORD’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the breadth of the address and the Chronicler’s use of “all Israel” for those in Judah and Benjamin. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that God’s word claims the whole community, not only its leaders.

verses.text: ‘The LORD says, “You shall not go up, nor fight against your brothers! Every man return to his house; for this thing is of me.” ’ ” So they listened to the LORD’s words, and returned from going against Jeroboam.
verses.arminianNotes: “You shall not go up, nor fight against your brothers… for this thing is of me,” and they obey. Arminian readers see a king and people freely heeding God’s word. Their obedience averts civil war and shows the value of listening to the prophets.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty and his people’s right response together, as “this thing is of me” names God’s hand in the division. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as clear shared ground about obeying God’s word and treating fellow Israelites as brothers, as in the notes on 1 Kings 12:24.

verses.text: Rehoboam lived in Jerusalem, and built cities for defense in Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam lives in Jerusalem and builds cities for defense in Judah. Arminian readers note that, having obeyed God’s word, the king turns to responsible stewardship of what remains. Prudent preparation is a fitting response to a dangerous situation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see wise action following obedience. This material has no parallel in Kings. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing a constructive response to the division, in which Rehoboam strengthens Judah rather than fighting his brothers.

verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam builds Bethlehem, Etam, and Tekoa. Arminian readers note that the list begins with towns in Judah’s heartland, including David’s hometown. The fortifications show careful planning for the security of a smaller kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the list as a record of defensive building. Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as historical description of Rehoboam’s fortifications, without seeking symbolic meaning in the names, and see in it the king’s concern for his people’s safety.

verses.arminianNotes: Beth Zur, Soco, and Adullam continue the list. Arminian readers note the spread of fortified towns across Judah’s hill country and lowlands. The record reflects the practical work of defense carried out under Rehoboam’s direction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the verse as part of a historical list. Shared ground: both traditions read it as describing the strengthening of Judah, and neither finds a doctrinal question in the geography.

verses.arminianNotes: Gath, Mareshah, and Ziph are named. Arminian readers note that the list includes towns toward the western lowlands and the south. The fortifications show how Rehoboam sought to secure the borders of his kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the names as part of the defensive network. Shared ground: both traditions treat the verse as historical detail, and both caution against drawing conclusions about the exact location or history of each town beyond what the text states.

verses.arminianNotes: Adoraim, Lachish, and Azekah are named. Arminian readers note the inclusion of Lachish, a significant town in later history. The list continues the record of Rehoboam’s careful preparation for defense.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as part of the list of fortified cities. Shared ground: both traditions treat it as historical description and see in the fortifications a king seeking to protect the people entrusted to him.

verses.text: Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron, which are fortified cities in Judah and in Benjamin.
verses.arminianNotes: Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron complete the list of fortified cities in Judah and Benjamin. Arminian readers note that Hebron, David’s first royal city, is included. The fortified network spans both tribes that remained loyal to David’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the mention of Judah and Benjamin together. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as summarizing Rehoboam’s defensive building, and both see in it the consolidation of the kingdom that remained under David’s line.

verses.text: He fortified the strongholds and put captains in them with stores of food, oil and wine.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam fortifies the strongholds, appoints captains, and stocks food, oil, and wine. Arminian readers note the thoroughness of his preparations. Responsible leadership includes practical provision for the people’s defense and needs.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see prudent administration in these measures. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing wise preparation, and both affirm that such practical care is compatible with trust in God, as long as it does not replace it.

verses.text: He put shields and spears in every city, and made them exceedingly strong. Judah and Benjamin belonged to him.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam puts shields and spears in every city and makes them very strong; Judah and Benjamin belong to him. Arminian readers note that the kingdom is now secure. Yet strength can lead to complacency, as 12:1 will show, and they read the verse with that in view.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the kingdom’s strength and the later warning that strength preceded unfaithfulness (12:1). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a high point in Rehoboam’s reign and see in it a reminder that security is a gift to be used faithfully.

verses.text: The priests and the Levites who were in all Israel stood with him out of all their territory.
verses.arminianNotes: The priests and Levites from all Israel stand with Rehoboam. Arminian readers note that they choose loyalty to the LORD’s worship over their homes in the north. Their decision is a costly act of faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the priests and Levites aligning with the temple and David’s house. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of faithfulness to God’s appointed worship, and both see in it the beginning of a movement that strengthened Judah.

verses.text: For the Levites left their pasture lands and their possessions, and came to Judah and Jerusalem; for Jeroboam and his sons cast them off, that they should not execute the priest’s office to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The Levites leave their pasture lands and possessions because Jeroboam and his sons cast them off from serving as priests to the LORD. Arminian readers note the sacrifice involved. They give up property and security to remain faithful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see costly faithfulness and note Jeroboam’s responsibility for driving them out. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as honoring the Levites’ willingness to suffer loss for the sake of true worship, a theme that would encourage the returned community.

verses.text: He himself appointed priests for the high places, for the male goat and calf idols which he had made.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeroboam appoints his own priests for the high places, for the goat and calf idols he made. Arminian readers note that Jeroboam deliberately replaces God’s appointed worship with his own. 1 Kings 12:28–31 describes the calves and the non-Levitical priests.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Jeroboam’s worship as a serious departure from God’s commands. Chronicles adds the goat idols (compare Leviticus 17:7). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober account of false worship, for which Jeroboam bears responsibility.

verses.text: After them, out of all the tribes of Israel, those who set their hearts to seek the LORD, the God of Israel, came to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: After them, from all the tribes of Israel, those who set their hearts to seek the LORD come to Jerusalem to sacrifice. Arminian readers see sincere seekers responding to God and choosing faithful worship, even at cost. Their hearts are set on the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same seekers and attribute their seeking to God’s grace at work in their hearts. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a beautiful picture of faithful worshipers from every tribe drawn to the LORD’s house, and neither turns it into a dispute about the source of their seeking.

verses.text: So they strengthened the kingdom of Judah and made Rehoboam the son of Solomon strong for three years, for they walked three years in the way of David and Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes: These newcomers strengthen Judah and make Rehoboam strong for three years, while they walk in the way of David and Solomon. Arminian readers note that faithfulness brings blessing, and that the limit of three years hints at what follows in 12:1.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the blessing that accompanies faithful worship and the warning implied by its brevity. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that seeking the LORD strengthens his people, and that continued faithfulness is needed to keep that strength.
